title: Rebellious Children and the Futile Help of Egypt
summary: The LORD pronounces woe on Judah's leaders for sending envoys and treasure to Egypt without asking him, calling Egypt "Rahab Who Sits Still," a monster that does nothing. Isaiah is told to write down the message as a witness against a people who want only pleasant prophecies and who refused the salvation offered in repentance and rest. Yet the LORD longs to be gracious: he will answer their cry, guide them, heal their wounds, and shatter Assyria with his voice.
story: This is the third woe of chapters 28 to 33, and here the hidden plans of 29:15 come into the open. Judah's leaders are negotiating an alliance with Egypt against Assyria. The chapter sets out the choice that runs through Isaiah's ministry: trust in the LORD or trust in horses, armies, and foreign powers. It has two halves of nearly equal length. Verses 1 to 17 condemn the Egyptian alliance and the refusal to listen; verses 18 to 33 turn to God's grace toward his people and his judgment on Assyria. Chapter 31 will repeat the warning in a shorter form, and chapters 36 and 37 will show the crisis itself.
historical:
The setting is almost certainly the years leading to Sennacherib's invasion of 701 BC. After the death of the Assyrian king Sargon II in 705 BC, Hezekiah withheld tribute from Assyria and joined a coalition of rebel states, looking to Egypt for military support. Egypt at this time was ruled by a dynasty of kings from Kush (the Nile valley south of Egypt, in modern Sudan), who were eager to limit Assyrian power in the Levant. Zoan (verse 4) was the city later known as Tanis, in the northeastern Nile Delta, an important royal center. Hanes has not been securely identified; many scholars place it at Heracleopolis in Middle Egypt, though other locations have been proposed.

Isaiah's warning proved true. When Sennacherib marched west in 701 BC, an Egyptian force met him at Eltekeh, near the coast, and was defeated, according to Sennacherib's own annals. Judah's fortified cities fell one after another, and Jerusalem was spared only by the LORD's intervention (37:36-37). The Rabshakeh's taunt in 36:6, that Egypt was a splintered reed that would pierce the hand of anyone who leaned on it, repeats Isaiah's own verdict from the other side.
cultural:
Verse 6 pictures a caravan crossing the Negev, the dry region south of Judah, with donkeys and camels loaded with gifts for Egypt. Tribute and gifts were how small kingdoms bought alliances, and sending them through a desert full of lions and snakes shows how costly and desperate the mission was. Rahab (not the woman of Jericho, whose name is spelled differently in Hebrew) was the name of a mythic sea monster, a symbol of chaos, and Israel's poets applied it to Egypt (Psalm 87:4; Isaiah 51:9). Isaiah gives the monster a humiliating nickname: it only sits.

Writing on a tablet and a scroll (verse 8) created a lasting public record that could be checked later, as ancient treaties and legal documents were. Verse 14 draws on the potter's shop: broken pottery was so common that a sizable shard was normally useful for carrying coals or scooping water, but Judah will be shattered beyond even that. Topheth (verse 33) was a place in the Valley of Hinnom, just outside Jerusalem, associated with child sacrifice (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31). Isaiah turns it into the funeral pyre prepared for the Assyrian king, a grim image of total judgment.
literary: The chapter is built on reversals of the people's own words. They wanted "shelter under Pharaoh's protection" (verse 2), and that protection becomes their shame. They say they will flee on horses, so they will flee (verse 16). They tell the prophets to stop seeing visions and to get the Holy One of Israel out of their way (verses 10 and 11), so Isaiah answers with a message from "the Holy One of Israel" (verse 12). Verse 15 is the chapter's center, a one-line summary of Isaiah's teaching: salvation lies in turning back and resting, strength in quietness and trust, "but you were not willing." The word "therefore" in verse 18 then opens a surprising turn: because the people refused, the LORD waits to be gracious. The last section (verses 27 to 33) is a theophany, a poetic description of God's coming in storm and fire, with the image of the Name of the LORD coming from afar.

outline.t: Woe to the rebellious children who go down to Egypt
The caravan through the Negev and Rahab Who Sits Still
A written witness against a people who refuse the truth
The LORD longs to be gracious: guidance, rain, and healing
The LORD comes in fire to shatter Assyria

doctrines.note: Verse 15 defines saving faith in Isaiah's terms: turning back to God and resting, quietness and trust, instead of frantic self-help. The people's alternative, horses and foreign alliances, looks strong but fails.

The Hebrew word for repentance in verse 15 means returning. Salvation begins with turning back to the God the people had walked away from, and the chapter shows how he keeps the door open even after they refuse.

The people want prophets who speak pleasant words and illusions (verse 10). God's word is written down as a lasting witness (verse 8), and later he promises that his people will hear his guidance plainly (verse 21).

words.note: Shuvah, returning or repentance. This noun appears only here in the Old Testament, but it comes from shuv, the common verb for turning back. In verse 15 it stands beside rest as the path of salvation: turning away from false trust and toward God.

Rahab, a name for a sea monster of chaos in Hebrew poetry (Job 26:12; Psalm 89:10), and a poetic name for Egypt. In verse 7 Isaiah gives it a mocking title: the great monster that sits still. Egypt looks formidable but will do nothing.

Chanan, to be gracious, to show favor. Verses 18 and 19 use it three times. Grace here is God's undeserved kindness to people who have just refused him, and it is active: he rises to show compassion and answers when they cry.

christ: Verse 21 promises a voice that says "This is the way. Walk in it," and verse 20 speaks of a Teacher who will no longer hide. Many translations read teachers in the plural, and the Hebrew can mean either; Christians have heard in it the hope of God himself teaching his people, which the New Testament sees fulfilled in Jesus, who calls himself the way (John 14:6), and in the Spirit who guides into truth (John 16:13). The link is thematic rather than a direct prophecy. More broadly, the chapter's call to quiet trust instead of self-reliance runs through Jesus' teaching, and his invitation to the weary to find rest (Matthew 11:28-29) answers the rest that Judah refused in verse 15.

hard.q: Wasn't seeking an alliance with Egypt simply prudent statecraft? Why does Isaiah treat it as sin?
hard.a:
From a political point of view, Hezekiah's advisers had good reasons. Assyria was brutal, Egypt was a major power with its own interest in resisting it, and small kingdoms routinely survived by making alliances. Isaiah's objection is not that diplomacy is wicked in itself. It is that the plan was made "without asking My advice" (verse 2), that it rested Judah's security on a foreign power rather than on the LORD, and that it was pursued in the face of prophetic warning. Alliances in the ancient world were sealed with oaths before the gods of both parties, so a treaty with Egypt was also a statement of trust.

The events bore Isaiah out: Egypt's help at Eltekeh failed, and Judah was devastated. Readers still disagree about how directly the chapter applies to modern politics. What it plainly teaches is that God's people are not to place in any human power the trust that belongs only to him.

questions: Verse 15 says strength lies in quietness and trust. Why is this so hard to believe when a crisis hits?
The people told their prophets to speak pleasant words. In what ways do people today choose teachers who tell them what they want to hear?
Verse 18 says the LORD longs to be gracious even after being refused. How does that change the way someone who has refused God can approach him?
